description: This is a market on the likelihood of a military clash between China and India occurring by December 31.

eventMetadata.context_description: Recent high-level boundary talks in Beijing on August 25, 2026, produced an eight-point consensus between India’s National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi. The sides reaffirmed commitments to maintain peace and tranquility along the Line of Actual Control, established two new military hotlines and additional commander-level meeting points in the eastern and middle sectors, and tasked expert groups with advancing boundary delimitation toward an early harvest. These steps build on post-2024 disengagement and follow earlier diplomatic exchanges ahead of potential leadership meetings, including a possible Xi visit during the September BRICS summit. Isolated reports of patrols or alleged activity in Arunachal Pradesh were denied by Indian officials and described as stable but requiring vigilance. Enhanced communication channels and scheduled follow-up talks in India in 2027 provide structured mechanisms to address disputes and reduce miscalculation risks along the disputed Himalayan frontier.

markets.description:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if there is a military encounter between the military forces of China (People's Republic of China) and India between January 29, 2025 and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

A "military encounter" is defined as any incident involving the use of force such as missile strikes, artillery fire, exchange of gunfire, or other forms of direct military engagement between Chinese and Indian military forces. Hand-to-hand combat with the use of melee weapons between military personnel, will qualify. For example the 2020 Galwan Valley clash and the 2022 Yangtse clash would both count.

Non-violent actions, such as warning shots, artillery fire into uninhabited areas, or missile launches that land in territorial waters or pass through airspace, will not qualify for a "Yes" resolution. Intentional ship ramming that results in significant damage to (e.g., a hole in the hull) or the sinking of a military ship by another will count toward a "Yes" resolution, however minor damage (scrapes, dents) will not.

Note: the China Coast Guard (CCG) is part of the military, however the Indian Coast Guard (ICG) is not.

The resolution source for this market will be a consensus of credible reporting.
